nameStory: The Long-horned Sandmole gets its curious name from its habitat and appearance - it burrows through sandy sediments like a tiny mole, while its long antennae stick out like horns. Despite the name, it's not a mole at all, but a marine crustacean that 'swims' through sand much like a mole moves through soil.
description: The Long-horned Sandmole is a small, flattened marine crustacean that lives buried in sandy ocean floors along New England's coast. This pale, translucent creature grows to about half an inch long and has a distinctly oval, pill bug-like body. Its most striking feature is a pair of exceptionally long antennae that can extend nearly as long as its entire body. Like other isopods, it has seven pairs of legs and breathes through gills, making it more closely related to terrestrial pill bugs than to any actual mole.

idTips.label: Extra-long antennae
idTips.description: Two thread-like antennae extend forward from the head, often as long as the entire body length, feeling delicate and flexible when gently touched

idTips.label: Flattened oval body
idTips.description: Body is distinctly flattened top-to-bottom with an oval outline, feeling firm but slightly yielding like a soft plastic bead

idTips.label: Pale translucent color
idTips.description: Overall whitish to pale gray color with a semi-transparent quality that lets you see internal structures as darker shadows

idTips.label: Seven leg pairs
idTips.description: Count seven pairs of small walking legs along the underside, each ending in a tiny claw that feels slightly scratchy on skin

idTips.label: Sandy habitat
idTips.description: Always found burrowed in clean, medium-grain sand that feels gritty between fingers, never in mud or on hard surfaces

habitat: Long-horned Sandmoles inhabit clean, well-sorted sandy sediments in shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to about 30 feet deep. They prefer areas with moderate water movement that keeps the sand oxygenated, often found near sandy beaches, shallow bays, and sandy areas between rocky reefs. In New England, they're most common in protected coastal areas from Cape Cod northward where fine to medium sand accumulates.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, easier to find when sieving sand during low tides. Look for their tiny burrow openings in wet sand.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be encountered during beach seining or while digging for clams in sandy areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Late fall storms may wash them ashore after disturbance.
seasonality.winter: Retreat deeper into sediments and become less active, making them very difficult to find during this season.

funFact: Long-horned Sandmoles can actually 'swim' through sand by using their legs in a coordinated wave-like motion, moving through loose sediment almost as easily as a fish moves through water - they're essentially the submarines of the sandy seafloor!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small marine isopods, but the extremely long antennae are a dead giveaway - if the antennae are nearly as long as the body, you've found a Long-horned Sandmole. Remember: 'Long antennae, long name.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sandmole,' this creature is actually more closely related to the pill bugs (roly-polies) you find in your garden than to any mammal - they're both isopods, part of the diverse crustacean family that includes lobsters and crabs.
compareHints: **Note: Information about close relatives is uncertain due to limited reference material.** Long-horned Sandmoles can be distinguished from other small marine isopods by their exceptionally long antennae and preference for burrowing in clean sand rather than living on hard surfaces or in muddy areas. Most other coastal isopods have much shorter antennae and are found crawling on rocks, seaweed, or pier pilings rather than buried in sediment.
